title: Erdős Problem #1208
description: Erdős Problem #1208 (solved). Let $F_d(n)$ be the minimal size of a distinct-distance subset guaranteed to exist in any $n$-point set in $\mathbb{R}^d$. The problem asks for the asymptotics of $F_d(n)$ for fixed $d$ as $n \to \infty$. Formalization pending.

overview.historicalContext: Erdős posed this problem as a quantitative strengthening of the distinct distances problem. Given any $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$, what is the minimum size of a subset where all pairwise distances are distinct? Erdős noted a trivial lower bound of $F_d(n) \ge c \cdot n^{1/(d-1)}$ and conjectured sharper asymptotics. For $d = 2$, the problem is related to the Erdős distinct distances problem (how many distinct distances must any $n$ points determine), resolved by Guth and Katz in 2015. A greedy construction shows $F_d(n) \ge \Omega(n^{1/2})$ for all $d$, and for points on a line $F_d(n) = n$ (all distances distinct by general position). The problem is marked as solved on erdosproblems.com, though the formalization is pending.
overview.problemStatement: For $d\geq 2$ let $F_d(n)$ be minimal such that every set of $n$ points in $\mathbb{R}^d$ contains a set of $F_d(n)$ points with distinct distances. Estimate $F_d(n)$ for fixed $d$ as $n\to \infty$.

A full formalization would require: (1) defining $F_d(n)$ as the minimum over all $n$-point configurations of the maximum distinct-distance subset size; (2) proving upper and lower bound matching asymptotically; (3) using Mathlib's `EuclideanSpace`, `Finset.card`, and combinatorial tools.
keyInsights: $F_d(n)$ is defined as: $\min_{|P|=n} \max\{|S| : S \subseteq P, \text{ all pairwise distances in } S \text{ distinct}\}$. It is the worst-case guaranteed size of a distinct-distance subset.

A greedy algorithm gives $F_d(n) \ge \Omega(n^{1/2})$: pick points one at a time, each new point creates at most $k-1$ new distances equal to existing ones, so after $k$ steps the 'conflicts' are at most $k^2$, which must be $\le n$.

For $d \ge 2$, the distinct distances problem (how many distinct distances $n$ points must determine) gives a lower bound on $F_d(n)$: more distinct distances means larger distinct-distance subsets are easier to find.
On a line (1D case), any $n$ points can be perturbed to have all $\binom{n}{2}$ distances distinct. In higher dimensions, degenerate configurations (e.g., all points on a circle) can limit $F_d(n)$.
